Clause 6.3 - there is no need to amend this, the provision already includes (but is not limited to) unlawful activity (they are asking for “illegal” - same thing); breach of agreement and fraud is also expressly included. Hi [~accountid:5f5b93718d3ae70076d6b271]. Yes, that’s correct. Basically the process goes like this:

* We get the _public_ part of their PGP keypair
* We encrypt the message and attachments using their public key
* We send over the encrypted message and attachments to them over email
* They can then decrypt and extract the message & data with their _private_ key

This way no one except the holder of the private key can decrypt the data. Even if the email is somehow intercepted and its contents captured by a malicious third party, it is only encrypted data that is unreadable.

Hi [~accountid:61027999ec92ab00707f6ac1] 

Thanks for raising this issue.

Unfortunately, taking this website down involves considerable costs - up to 10K EUR, unless the domain name registrant will not abandon it voluntarily.

# .ru whois does not reveal who is the registrant, it only mentions ‘private person’. Thus, we need to request the registrant’s details (name, email) from the relevant registrar. For obtaining this information, we should use a local IP law firm. Relevant costs are ca 400 EUR, which do not include expenses such as notarisation and translation of a PoA and courier costs for delivering original documents. Please also note that due to the recent case-law in Russia, the registrar may refuse to issue these details based on privacy laws.
# Domain name disputes are considered as trademark infringement cases in Russia. If we succeed to obtain the registrant details, the second step would be sending a cease and desist letter to the registrant. Related costs are 800-1000 EUR.
# If the registrant does not reply to our letter, the next step is a court action against the registrant.  A simple alternative dispute resolution does not exist. The court case costs ca 8K EUR.

Taking into account the high costs, I think it is not worth to proceed with this case. 

Please let us know if you have any comments or additional questions.  

Best regards,

Indrek

The reason for the issue was in misconfiguration of replication. 

There’s such a thing as {{partitioning}} in [replication configuration|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENGINEERING/pages/4049731679/How+to+setup+self-serve+replication+to+Delta+Lake#Target]. It is responsible for checking the immutability of the row. We had it configured as {{BYDATE}} which means we check this row value to decide if replicated data should be updated. You can check *Semantic of Uniqueness of the row* section of provided doc and it describes our case.

To solve the issue it’s enough to set {{partitionType: "NONE"}} and drop {{partitionColumn}}

To clarify, I called “spending” to the difference between “gross earnings” and “net earnings” of the driver… “Expenses” is the correct word in english used in the App. 

Continuing with the 10€ example; when the refund happens, then the driver will see “-10€” in the “expenses” section under the title of “refund to client”, and also a decrease of 10€ in his net earnings. So the client receives back his 10€ directly deducted from driver’s net earnings.  

*In driver’s balance, as the “gross income” will not be reduced in 10€ as I believe it should, then the commission will still be charged and it will be deducted for the driver’s next payout.*

So, the outcome of all this situation is that client has his 10€ back; Bolt keeps his 1.5€; and driver will be -1.5 after this refund.

Finally, I confirm that, in this example, the loss / spending for the driver will not be (8.50+1.50=10 euros), but 11.50€.

DPO Advice:

After reviewing this DPIA, it is suggested that the following items need to be checked/corrected:

* Lack of explicit retention period: Bolt must indicate explicitly a retention period for the data processed. If it is not possible to determine the exact period in advance, the criteria for why such a period has not been explicitly defined should be indicated (e.g., “keeping the data for the duration of the contractual relationship”).

* Lack of indication of secondary purposes: It has been indicated in some parts of the DPIA that data may be kept for possible fraud issues. This is a secondary use of the data, which needs to be made explicit in the DPIA (and there is no reference to the criteria present in Art. 6(4) GDPR regarding the use of data for secondary purposes).

* Absence of information on contracts with data processors: there needs to be an indication as to whether there are any contracts with one of the data processors located outside the EEA.

* No risk analysis in international transfers: no indication of what mechanism for international data transfer is used in the relationship with the data processor located in India. There is also no reference to any Transfer Impact Assessments on international transfers.

This is something we are are working on currently - finding a way to raise the activity while still remaining a platform. The same question is relevant for all the Baltic states.

As a general rule, the platform should be providing means to an end.

There is currently pan-European legislation in works, that is connected to reclassification risk. In the current wording, if 2 of 5 criteria is met, the person could be considered an employee:

(a)effectively determining, or setting upper limits for the level of remuneration;

_Applicable for us_

(b)requiring the person performing platform work to respect specific binding rules with regard to appearance, conduct towards the recipient of the service or performance of the work;

_Not applicable_

(c)supervising the performance of work or verifying the quality of the results of the work including by electronic means;

_Applicable for us_

(d)effectively restricting the freedom, including through sanctions, to organise one’s work, in particular the discretion to choose one’s working hours or periods of absence, to accept or to refuse tasks or to use subcontractors or substitutes;

_Not applicable_

(e)effectively restricting the possibility to build a client base or to perform work for any third party.

_Not applicable_

The ideal solution would be that we would control the quality and price, but we can have -in my opinion- one or the other. I think the price criteria already has some preliminary solution (I think I have seen how the driver makes a counter-offer for a higher price).

As [~accountid:5e343c77a7f27d0e6c6d6698] suggested I have tried to calculate manually all fields based on 5 digits after point.

So as initial setup we have two row values with sum_with_vat: 0.8 and 2.0 and vat percentage 20%

sum  without vat for rows (sum_with_vat * 100 / (100 + vat_percentage)):

0.8*100/(100 + 20) = 0.66667 ~ 0.67

2.0*100/(100 + 20) = 1.66667 ~ 1.67

now we can calculate vat amount for individual row (sum_with_vat - sum_without_vat):

0.8 - 0.66667 = 0.13333 ~ 0.13

2.0 - 1.66667 = 0.33332 ~ 0.33



Based on this values we can calculate total values:

total_sum_with_vats: 0.8 + 2.0 = 2.8

total_sum_without_vat = 0.66667 + 1.66667 = 2.33334 ~ 2.33

total_vat_sum = 2.8 - 2.33334 = 0.466659 ~ 0.47



Compare rounded values:

total sum: 0.67 + 1.67 != 2.33

total vats: 0.13 + 0.33 != 0.47



In case we round sum values that we get during calculation before calculating total_sum the result will be the following:

total_sum_with_vats: 0.8 + 2.0 = 2.8

total_sum_without_vat: 0.67 + 1.67 = 2.34

total_vat_sum: 2.8 - 2.34 = 0.45999 ~ 0.46 (that is js magic)



So from my perspective increase number of digits after point will not fix all existing problems that we have right now. And removing vat amout from rows will partially fix issue however user can manually perform sum_with_vats - sum_without_vat from individual row and get vat values for individual row and in case we still have total vat amount then user/client can came to us saying that values are still incorrect

*Summary: Legal analysis shows that Bolt’s verticals (especially for Food, Market and Rides) are online marketplaces, and thus Bolt falls under the scope of NIS2.*

On 16 January 2023, the[ |https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32022L2555&from=EN][+Directive (EU) 2022/2555+|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32022L2555&from=EN] (known as NIS2) entered into force replacing Directive (EU) 2016/1148. NIS2 aims to:

* set minimum rules regarding the functioning of a coordinated regulatory framework;

* lay down mechanisms for effective cooperation among the responsible authorities in each Member State;

* update the list of sectors and activities subject to cybersecurity obligations (see annexes);

* provide effective remedies and enforcement measures which are key to the effective enforcement of those obligations.

Simply put, the companies that fall under the scope of NIS2 would be companies that:

* employ more than 250 persons, have annual turnover more than EUR 50 million, and/or an annual balance sheet total exceeding EUR 43 million;

* operate within the sectors and provide the types of service listed in 

[ |https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32022L2555&from=EN][+NIS2 annexes+|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32022L2555&from=EN].

NIS2 Annex II names “digital providers“ that would be:

* providers of online marketplaces

* providers of online search engines

* providers of social networking services platforms

Bolt’s Food and Market vertical would clearly fall into the “providers of online marketplaces“ definition, because Bolt is an online intermediation services provider that offers business users (restaurants, producers and distributors) the opportunity to propose goods or services to consumers and which have the aim of facilitating transactions between business users and consumers.

Bolt Rides would fall under NIS2 directive “providers of online marketplaces”, because:

* in essence it does intermediates driver’s and passenger’s transactions on its platform;

* Under Digital Services Act (DSA) legal product counsels have advised for Bolt Rides to be considered as “online marketplaces”, as otherwise we would be categorised as transport service providers which would bring along several unsuitable obligations together with reclassifications risk of the drivers. Thus, as under one legislative document (DSA) we have stated that we are “providers of online marketplaces“, then we have to do the same also under another (NIS2).

The Member States have 21 months in order to transpose NIS2 to their national legislative framework.

* Both sns/sqs name *should end* with {{.fifo}}  suffix
* Both sns/sqs in subscription should be FIFO
* By default, message [should contain deduplication ID|https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/using-messagededuplicationid-property.html] (based on it message will be delivered once), or you can set  {{content_based_deduplication = true}}  in terraform for SQS and then deduplication will be done based on message content
* 1,000 FIFO sns per account
* 100 subscriptions per topic
* SNS throughput: 300 messages per second or 10 MB per second, per topic, whichever comes first
* SQS throughput: Without batching, FIFO queues support up to 300 API calls per second, If you use [batching|https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-batch-api-actions.html], FIFO queues support up to 3,000 calls per second, per API method

*This is our Idea FAQ:* 
Sabia que é possível receber faturas automáticas das deslocações feitas com Perfil Fiscal? Cada vez que pagar com o Perfil Fiscal, será enviada uma fatura digital pré-preenchida para um email à sua escolha. Bastam alguns passos para criar e usar um Perfil Fiscal de forma gratuita.

*Como é que crio um Perfil Fiscal?*

* Na app da Bolt, abrir o menu e selecionar Pagamento;
* No fundo da página, clicar em Configurar Perfil Fiscal;
* Seguir as instruções no ecrã, adicionando o email (onde vai receber as faturas) e um método de pagamento.

_Nota: Pode alterar os dados fiscais sempre que quiser clicando em Editar Perfil Profissional (??) no Menu Pagamentos._

*Viajar com um Perfil Fiscal*

Selecione o Perfil Fiscal como método de pagamento *ANTES* de qualquer deslocação, para que no final seja automaticamente enviada uma fatura com os dados fiscais para um email à escolha. Ou seja, rápido, fácil e sem complicações — como deve ser!

*Aceda às suas faturas com os dados fiscais*

Vais receber a fatura da viagem no teu email, onde podes descarregá-la na opção Descarregar fatura em PDF. Se não conseguires encontrar o email na Caixa de Entrada ou no Spam, podes solicitar um novo envio da fatura. Para isso, vai a As minhas viagens, seleciona a viagem pretendida e toca em Reenviar a fatura.

*NB:* Saiba que pode levar até 24 horas depois de uma viagem para que o NIF seja adicionado ao uma fatura de trabalho.

Por último, a alteração dos dados de uma fatura é um processo manual e poderá demorar. Por isso, é importante que tenha um Perfile Fiscal criado e que o mesmo está selecionado antes de cada viagem.

Hi Viktoriia,

Thanks for reaching out.

There is no need for fraud blocks to be implemented by agents from other teams.

In general, blocking the account should suffice. We have the operational tools and background to assess whether a device UID should be blocked or blacklisted, effectively disabling many other users from using our services.

However, as different blocks have been developed for different types of bad behaviour, some might include this action. Every team has access to those blocks that they would have a valid use for.

Generally, one rider making fake orders is not a situation that we would advise taking manual action on anyway. We have rules in place that will detect fraudulent behaviour, they will be rejected or challenged at the order request checkpoint and related users will have this related blacklisted user/instrument in their input. 

I hope that this has been helpful and please don’t hesitate to write to us again if there is anything else that would help to be clarified/discussed.

Cheers,
Francesca

For background, there are 2 types of data request usually:

* *Trip data request from a local authority that is the same as the driver/vehicle*

* i.e. Wolverhampton council asking for trip data of a trip conducted by a Wolverhampton driver/vehicle
* We are usually required by our private hire operator licence to keep this information and make it available for inspection on request by council officers/police etc…
* Our historical approach of this has been (and to my understanding) that given it is a licence condition, the local authority/police’s powers to inspect it is comes derives from our obligations under the licence therefore a DPA and the relevant justifications don’t necessarily need to be provided

* *Trip data request from a local authority that is* *_different_* *to the driver/vehicle*

* This is what has happened in this instance, where a Manchester City Council officer has asked for trip data of a trip conducted by a Wolverhampton driver/vehicle
* The advice I have given from a regulatory side is that in my view, the Manchester council doesn’t have authority to request data on trip that is undertaken based on our private hire in Wolverhampton (with an exception)
* The reference by the Manchester City Council officer about having to assist council officers from other council is *incorrectly advised* as it pertains to trips that have been sub-contracted (i.e. Bolt Wolverhampton accepted it then sub-contracts it to Bolt Manchester to be allocated to a Bolt Manchester driver - this is not the case and not applicable to Bolt’s operations as we do not sub-contract.)
* The exception to the trip data request is that our approach is ask for a DPA and it’s a sufficiently serious issue such as touting/plying for hire (which is usually the case) then I do ask the team to try and provide it given the justification of a touting/plying for hire sanction from the council side is that they will likely suspend/revoke/prosecute the driver.

* Touting: Where a driver essentially herds a passenger into their cab to book it
* Plying for hire: Where a driver takes a trip that isn’t booked through an operator like Bolt
* Normally these type of trip data request is used as evidence to prove plying for hire or touting because a driver most likely claimed it’s a Bolt trip when they are plying for hire so there shouldn’t be any records on our side/touting where there was a trip based on the passenger’s complaint.

So in this specific circumstance, given Liina’s question to you:

{quote}_Should we accept the formatting - it’s not signed and stamped, but it might be digitally signed, so all ok?_{quote}

* I’m afraid I can’t answer that Q re validity of the DPA.

{quote}_Is there a reference to a provision to a relevant law that authorises them to request the info- I can’t really read out that part?_{quote}

* As per the second type of trip request above, there is no specific provision for Manchester City Council to be requesting trip data of a Wolverhampton driver. They have been incorrectly advised which we will correct on our side.
* Per the above, there is *no* specific law for this specific authority (i.e. Manchester) to request this trip data, however, our usual approach has been that if the DPA is valid with the valid justification (i.e. prosecution/suspension/revocation for a serious offence such as plying for hire or touting) then we have provided the information in the past.

{quote}_Should we sign the witness statement form as an operator representative?_{quote}

* We have signed these in the past, they have been done by myself or [@jason.camilleri|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U8XPJA2ES] historically, to avoid an massive operational burden, we usually ask what the witness statements are for and confirm that they will be used for prosecution (Case Managers will handle those sort of comms)

As I mentioned above, the campaign (giving prizes) will result in additional tax cost for Bolt:

* There will be a corporation tax cost of 20% on the value of prizes for Bolt Operations OU in Estonia; 
* There is likely to be a VAT cost relating to the prizes, either by means of non-deductible input VAT and/or accounting for output VAT. Typically, only prizes of low value (e.g. under €10) would not result in adverse VAT consequences. The VAT rate and the exact consequences depend on the country of the supply, i.e. where the winner is located. 
* We haven’t considered the personal income tax consequences for the winners, and, as such, this remains solely with the winners themselves. This has been caveated in the global T&Cs shared by [~accountid:6052891960d39e006f72f0f0] . 

In order to mitigate any withholding tax and/or employment tax risks, it is important that the campaign is run by Bolt Operations OU and not the local support entity. The global T&Cs shared by [~accountid:6052891960d39e006f72f0f0] support this, however, please ensure that this is adhered to in practice. The cost of the campaign, including the cost relating to the prizes should be booked directly in the P&L of Bolt Operations OU (and not in the P&L of the local entity with the subsequent recharge of this cost to Bolt Operations OU).

Please see my comments below: 

* Corporation tax - in order to calculate the corporation tax due, the value of the prize must be “grossed” up in Estonia for Bolt Operations OU. So if the total value of the prizes is €2,340, the tax due on this will be €585 (€2,340 x20/80).  
* VAT - this depends on the type of prize and where it will be issued. Is the VAT already included in the value of the prize or will be added on top of it (i.e. when the invoice will be issued to Bolt by the supplier, which amount will be included there)? If it is included, there should be no additional VAT cost to consider for budgeting purposes. If the amounts don’t include VAT, you can expect the following: 
** Romania - no input VAT deduction for Bolt, resulting in 19% VAT cost for Bolt
** Poland - no input VAT deductibility for Bolt, resulting in 23% VAT cost for Bolt
** Czech Republic - no input VAT deduction for Bolt, resulting in 21% VAT cost for Bolt
** Lithuania - since the prize is a multi-purpose voucher, there shouldn’t be any VAT due upon issuance, MVP shall only be subject to VAT when it is redeemed (i.e., by the winner in our case)
** Kenya - no input VAT deduction for Bolt, resulting in 16% VAT cost for Bolt
* The local entity is essentially the Bolt’s group company in the relevant territory. Any invoices should be addressed to Bolt Operations OU and not to the local entity.

[DLA Piper overview on Nepal|https://www.dlapiperdataprotection.com/index.html?t=law&c=NP]I identified the following:

# The Privacy Act and the Privacy Regulation do not establish a data protection authority or regulatory authority responsible for the administration and enforcement of privacy and data protection matters in Nepal. The current applicable laws do not require the registration for a data protection officer, notification or any other registration requirements.
# Furthermore, the Nepal Privacy Act is silent on extra-territorial applicability and is unclear on whether it is applicable on foreign entities not having physical presence in Nepal. From a strict interpretation of the Privacy Act, it does not seem to have extra-territorial applicability and is applicable only to entities having registered in or operating within Nepal.
# If the Privacy Act would still apply  to Bolt, then “consent” is the only possible basis for processing data. However neither the term 'consent' nor the procedure for obtaining it is defined.

4. A person, who commits an offence under the Privacy Act, is liable for a punishment of imprisonment of up to three years or a fine of up to NPR 30, 000 (approx. €220), or both (Section 29(2) of the Privacy Act). 

Conclusion: Based on the above I find that there are no immediate blockers for lightweight launch in Nepal from privacy.

Hey [~accountid:5fedbf73f7ea2a01077a3dd8], thanks a lot for your patience! We have discussed this within the team and started thinking to what extent is this feature different from the Driver Prioritisation feature? If it is different, then why have we dropped Driver Prioritisation feature?

All in all, there are three legal matters that we need to take into account while structuring this feature:

* *Transparency angle* - drivers need to know how they are dispatched, if we are prioritising some drivers to other drivers, then it needs to be clear for all drivers using our service. This would mean that we need to update the app copies and likely T&Cs.
* *Privacy angle* - we will be making automated decisions based on driver’s behaviour if this feature is applied. My understanding is that this is forbidden, unless it is needed for the performance of driver’s contract (T&Cs) with us. I am adding [~accountid:609f85c547ba02006fe1b9c3] here for visibility.
* *Reclassification angle* - as you most likely know, the authorities tend to want to reclassify our drivers as our employees. If this happens, we will be forced to pay drivers the benefits they are entitled to under employment agreements. Since these amounts are big, we would like to avoid / mitigate this risk.
** For now dispatching works based on a factor which does not control driver’s performance (distance from the rider).
** What we would want to do is to take into account 20+ features partially pertaining to driver’s behaviour on the platform. Depending on the weight of certain features in the score,  we will be most likely be monitoring driver’s performance on the platform and dispatching the driver who is the best performer. This means that we might be limiting access to the platform for certain drivers - some drivers will not be getting that many orders because they are bad performers.
*** What we can do to mitigate the risk? Take out all performance metrics from the score. Do you think that would be doable?

Hi all. We had a discussion this week with [~accountid:5f0ea3c39d9a1200294cef2c] to align on the best way forward for these requests. I’m aware there have been a number of different questions lately related to Bolt Market, some of which are not strictly legal questions and others which are EU-level questions. Following this discussion, we have agreed on an approach for how to deal with these requests, which broadly fall into 3 categories:

1. Requests such as this ticket, i.e. specific product restrictions/regulations, particularly for higher risk SKUs like alcohol, tobacco, medicines etc. *Given that these are country-specific, we ask that the Global Field Team takes the lead in completing these sheets with support from external legal counsel.* I am aware that some are quite specialist, and in some cases more regulatory than legal, so our suggestion is to outsource to (local) external counsel. 

2. Food safety/hygiene/operational compliance questions (e.g. food safety / storage / temperature requirements etc.). Although we receive a lot of questions like this, they are not really legal questions and so *we will be requesting that the Bolt Market team liaise directly with external service providers* in the relevant countries to address them going forward.

3. Broader questions on contractual restrictions/limitations and issues like competition/antitrust (e.g. the other tickets that you were assigned a while ago - I will flag in the tickets so we’re all on the same page). As mentioned on some of the other tickets, these are broader, often EU-level questions and so *we will handle these in the Product Legal team (with input from external counsel)*. To the extent that there are any national-level specifics, we will raise individual tickets on these in due course, but hope this would be one or two discrete questions rather than an entire sheet.

I hope this helps clear things up. Apologies for any confusion up to this point.

Thanks

Ben

Hey, Kristjan,

Client came back again regarding 4.2 still pushing towards their proposed addition. Question here aren’t their arguments covered by a) fact that user agrees to share data on individual level when registering in the Bolt application? b) employees spend company money, thus company has a right to see such information based on legitimate interest? New reasoning form their side below:

Dar kartą patikslinsime prašymą dėl 4.2. punkto:

* Telefono numeriai, informacija apie keliones ir už jas taikytini Paslaugų mokesčiai yra Vartotojų asmens duomenys (kaip apibrėžta ir Jūsų privatumo pranešime keleiviams ir važiuotojams).
* Mes prašome sutartyje apsibrėžti, kokiais asmens duomenimis tarp mūsų ir Jūsų, kaip atskirų duomenų valdytojų, bus keičiamasi vykdant sutartį. Būtent tuo tikslu mes ir siūlome sutartyje įrašyti 4.2. punktą.
* Jūsų privatumo pranešimas keleiviams ir važiuotojams, į kurį atsiuntėte nuorodą, nėra mūsų sutarties dalis. Tai yra informacijos pateikimas klientams/duomenų subjektams, kurį Jūs privalote atlikti pagal BDAR 13-14 str. Bet tai ne mūsų tarpusavio sutarties sudėtinė dalis, kadangi šio pranešimo turinį Jūs galite bet kada vienašališkai keisti, jo turinio mes niekaip neįtakojame, ir šią informaciją Jūs skelbiate duomenų subjektams savo nuožiūra, kaip atskiras duomenų valdytojas.
* Taip pat atkreipėme dėmesį, kad Jūsų privatumo pranešime keleiviams ir važiuotojams nėra nurodoma, kad jų asmens duomenys gali būti atskleisti kitiems Jūsų klientais, t.y. mums, „Bolt business“ paslaugų gavėjams. Jūsų informaciniame pranešime kaip galimi duomenų gavėjai yra minimi tik vairuotojai, „Bolt Operations OÜ“ grupės įmonės ir partneriai, o taip pat išoriniai duomenų gavėjai, su kuriais teisiškai privalote dalytis duomenimis, tokie kaip teisėsaugos ir priežiūros institucijos.
* Atsižvelgiant į tai, kad šiuo metu iš sutarties turinio nėra iki galo aiški asmens duomenų kuriais bus keičiamasi apimtis, yra svarbu ją apsibrėžti – taip užsitikrinsime pagal BDAR mums privalomo teisėtumo, sąžiningumo ir skaidrumo principo įgyvendinimą (BDAR 5 str. 1 d. (a)) , o taip pat išvengsime perteklinių asmens duomenų tvarkymo (duomenų kiekio mažinimo principas, BDAR 5 str. 1 d. (c)). Be to, aiškus duomenų apimties apsibrėžimas svarbus įgyvendinant ir atskaitomybės principą (BDAR 5 str. 2 d.).

Tikimės, kad atsižvelgiant į šiuos argumentus sutiksite papildyti sutartį mūsų siūlomu 4.2. punktu.

new query:

{code:sql}SELECT 
etl.city_id || ':' || etl.order_id AS KEY, 
1 AS ghost_ride
FROM ng_public_spark.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders etl
JOIN ng_public_spark.fraud_order_check foc ON etl.order_id = foc.order_id AND foc.city_id = etl.city_id
WHERE etl.created >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_DATE)
AND etl.created_date >= DATEADD(day, -10, CURRENT_DATE)
AND etl.payment_method_group = 'in-app'
AND etl.order_state = 'finished'
AND etl.order_type = 'rides'
AND foc.pickup_distance > 5000
AND foc.pickup_duration < 90 								-- combined with pickup distance > 5000 means the driver had an avg speed of over 200 km/h during the pickup
AND foc.ride_distance > 5000
AND foc.ride_duration < 180									-- combined with ride distance > 5000 means the driver had an avg speed of over 100 km/h during the ride
GROUP BY 1 {code}

count(*) AS count_rows
FROM analytics_staging.etl_driver_root_predicted_ltv_aggregated GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1

WITH first_id AS (
  SELECT
  p.id AS partner_id,
  MIN(d.id) AS first_driver_id
  FROM ng_public.fleet_driver_root AS p
  LEFT JOIN ng_public.fleet_driver AS d ON p.id = d.driver_root_id
  GROUP BY 1
  ),
  first_city as (
  SELECT
  partner_id,
  city_id AS first_city_id
  FROM first_id
  LEFT JOIN ng_public.fleet_driver AS d
  ON d.id = first_driver_id
  LEFT JOIN ng_public.fleet_company AS c
  ON d.company_id = c.id)
  SELECT 
  activation_date,
  count(*) AS count_rows,
  count(DISTINCT driver_root_id) AS count_distinct,
  round(sum(lifetime_1y_flv_gmv_eur + lifetime_1y_hlv_gmv_eur),2) AS total_ltv_eur,
  round(sum(lifetime_1y_flv_gmv_eur + lifetime_1y_hlv_gmv_eur)/count(driver_root_id),2) AS mean_ltv_eur,
  round(approx_percentile(lifetime_1y_flv_gmv_eur + lifetime_1y_hlv_gmv_eur, 0.5),2) AS median_ltv_eur
  FROM first_city
  LEFT JOIN ng_public.admin_system_city AS admin_system_city
  ON admin_system_city.id = first_city.first_city_id
  RIGHT JOIN analytics_staging.etl_driver_root_predicted_ltv_aggregated AS ltv ON ltv.driver_root_id  = first_city.partner_id
  WHERE country_code = 'pl' AND activation_date >= date '2022-01-01'
  GROUP BY 1{noformat}

Hi,

Thanks so much for the above info. 

According to Romanian law that transposed *NIS1*, by Digital Service Provider they also mean *online marketplace,* and the law *applies to providers who have established their headquarters on the territory of Romania*. We only have a local entity in RO, so I would assume the RO law does not cover us. Identification as a digital service provider is done through self-assessment. 

In what regards NIS2, just one comment on the above info:

_Bolt Rides would fall under NIS2 directive “providers of online marketplaces”, because:_

* _in essence it does intermediates driver’s and passenger’s transactions on its platform;_

* _Under Digital Services Act (DSA) legal product counsels have advised for Bolt Rides to be considered as “online marketplaces”, as otherwise we would be categorised as transport service providers which would bring along several unsuitable obligations together with reclassifications risk of the drivers. Thus, as under one legislative document (DSA) we have stated that we are “providers of online marketplaces“, then we have to do the same also under another (NIS2)._



Interesting. Because in 2017, the European Union Court of Justice decided that the services provided by apps such as Uber, connecting individuals with non-professional drivers, is covered by services in the field of transport and is not an information society service. Consequently, such a service must be excluded from the scope of the freedom to provide services in general as well as the directive on services in the internal market and the directive on electronic commerce.

Thank you!

Sorina

Daniel and Emilie explained that getting copies of the insurance certificate and policy details should be sufficient, Bolt should only worry about the insurance proof.

It should be for the fleet partner to worry that they have the correct doc in place with the car owner in order to be able to take correct insurance on the car.

Daniel explained that to insure smthg, you need to have a contractual interest or a financial interest → FO should have contractual interest.

Emilie checked the PT T&Cs and clause 4.3.4 do say that it’s the Fleet Partners' responsibility to ensure they’re insured and they have all mandatory insurances in place.

Art 12 of TVDE Law sets out that “Without prejudice to the other insurances required by law, the vehicles performing TVDE must have third party liability and personal accident insurance, including passengers transported and respective damages, in an amount not less than the minimum legally required for the activity of rental transport in light passenger motor vehicles.”

Art 14 of same law puts an obligation on the operator of the electronic platform “to ensure full and permanent compliance with the requirements for exercising the activity provided for in this law, including those relating to vehicles and TVDE service operators.”

Therefore we would like to ensure that we request the correct and necessary documents before registering new TVDE Fleet Operators on our Bolt platform.

At the moment, we ask to see 4 different documents in order to register a new TVDE vehicle on our platform:

* Vehicles' registration doc
* Insurance Certificate (green card)
* Insurance Conditions / Policy
* Inspection

*If the vehicle isn't owned by the Fleet, Fleet Owner can submit the original registration doc + rental agreement 

Regarding Law 45/2018, under clause 12, we can find the vehicles' requirements:

* Capacity <= 9
* Registration Plate from Portugal
* Age <= 7 years
* Yearly Inspection after completing 1 year old
* Insurance (50.000.000 Civil Liability + 10.000 Occupant Protection)

There is no particular statement regarding the vehicle's ownership. But we do find it important to have a clear view of the company's relationship with the vehicle (to avoid for example stolen cars riding with us).
